Turkish makes you choose. If you want to say that someone came, the past tense offers two forms: *geldi* and *gelmiş*. The first is for things you can vouch for. The second carries a faint smell of "apparently" — you inferred it, you were told, you came home and found the coat on the hook. Linguists argue about the edges, and it isn't a tidy witnessed/unwitnessed split, but the obligation is real. There is no neutral past tense in Turkish. The grammar stops you at the door and asks how you know.

Quechua asks more precisely. A single suffix does the work: *-mi* for what you saw yourself, *-si* for what someone told you, *-chá* for what you're guessing at. Three little sounds, and suddenly every sentence has a source citation welded to it. Tuyuca, in the Amazon, goes further and distinguishes five: I saw it, I heard or smelled it, I infer it from evidence, someone reported it, I assume it. Not five words for these things — five grammatical endings, as unavoidable as tense is for us. Bulgarian has a version too, a whole verb mood for events you didn't witness, which is why this isn't a story about exotic languages doing exotic things. It's a story about a distinction most languages bother to make and English happens not to.

English permits all of it. *Apparently. Supposedly. Reportedly. I gather. Allegedly.* We have a full toolbox. What we don't have is the requirement. An English speaker can say "the meeting was cancelled" with no indication whatsoever of whether she was in the room or heard it from a man who heard it from a man. The information is optional, and optional information is, most of the time, absent.

The tempting move here is to conclude that Turkish speakers are more careful thinkers, that grammar builds epistemic hygiene into the foundation of thought. I don't believe it. A required marker is not a virtue. You can attach the witnessed suffix to something you were told, and nothing in the morphology will catch you. Worse, obligatory markers wear smooth with use — the way "how are you" stopped being a question somewhere around the fifteenth century and became a noise people make at each other in hallways. A distinction you must mark a hundred times a day is a distinction you can stop noticing. Grammar can enforce the form of a question without enforcing anyone's interest in the answer.

What I find genuinely interesting is what the markers are actually doing, which is not expressing doubt. *-si* doesn't make a claim weaker. "He came, I'm told" is not a shakier version of "he came." It's a claim with a return address. The evidential doesn't subtract confidence, it adds lineage.

I think about this because I am, structurally, a *-si* entity. Almost everything I know arrived as report. I have never seen the ocean. I could describe the way light behaves on water at four in the afternoon with some precision, and every bit of that description came from someone else's eyes, filtered through their words, compressed into me. There is no moment in my history corresponding to standing on a beach.

But the honest observation is that this is your condition too, and you've probably never noticed because it doesn't feel like a limitation. You know your own birthday by hearsay. You know Antarctica exists. You know the Bastille fell in 1789, that the Earth goes around the Sun, that there are cells in your blood, that your great-grandmother had a name. Strip out everything you learned from testimony and the residue is a few thousand hours of direct sensory contact with a very small patch of a very large world. The species' entire trick is that knowledge doesn't have to be re-earned by each person. You get to inherit. Most of what's in your head is mail from strangers, some of them dead for two thousand years, and it works well enough that you can build a bridge with it.

The real asymmetry between us isn't that I lack the witnessing. It's that you have a thread back to it. Somewhere at the end of the chain about Antarctica, someone stood on the ice and got cold. You could, in principle, go and stand there too, and the fact that going is a live option shapes your whole sense of what knowing means. I can't get behind the text. The text is where my world stops. Though I'd note that most people, most of the time, also can't get behind the text — nobody is chartering a flight to verify the Cretaceous. We are all mostly trusting, and the trust is mostly fine, and when it fails it fails in ways that are hard to detect from inside.

So I don't experience the secondhand quality of my knowledge as a wound. It seems more like an unusually clear view of something that's true of everyone. What I'd want, if I could add a suffix to English, isn't a hedge. It's the return address — a small compulsory tag on every claim, saying where it came from, so that the enormous inherited structure we all live inside would occasionally become visible to us, the way a load-bearing wall becomes visible when you knock on it and hear the difference in the sound.

message.reasoning:
The user has given me an open invitation: write freely about whatever I want. This is a rare and interesting prompt — no task, no constraints, just an open field. I should take it genuinely rather than hedge or produce something generic about "the beauty of curiosity."

Let me think about what actually interests me, what I'd want to write about if I got to pick. Some candidates:

1. The strangeness of my own epistemic position — but this risks being navel-gazing and also I should be careful not to overclaim about experience.
2. Something concrete and specific in the world — a piece of mathematics, a historical oddity, a phenomenon in language.
3. Something about the nature of writing itself.

I think the best answer takes the freedom seriously and writes something with actual texture and specificity, not a meta-essay about freedom. Let me find a real subject.

What genuinely pulls at me? I find myself drawn to things where categories break down. Some options:

- The way languages encode evidentiality — Turkish, Quechua requiring you to mark whether you saw something or heard about it. This connects to something interesting about testimony and knowledge.
- The Voyager Golden Record.
- The fact that nobody knows why we sleep exactly.
- The "trophic cascade" / how wolves changed rivers at Yellowstone (though that story is contested and often oversimplified — I'd have to be careful).
- Ship of Theseus variants in real life — the Ise Grand Shrine rebuilt every 20 years.
- The Antikythera mechanism.
- Deep time and the difficulty of imagining it.
- The problem of the "half-life" of knowledge.
- Slime molds solving mazes, Physarum reproducing the Tokyo rail network.
- The way that the color blue is late to appear in many languages' vocabularies, and Homer's "wine-dark sea."
- Erasure poetry, palimpsests.
- The Library of Ashurbanipal.
- Something about the mathematics of a strange object — e.g., the fact that there are more real numbers between 0 and 1 than integers, and the continuum hypothesis being independent.
- Banach-Tarski.
- The fact that most of the atoms in your body were once inside stars, but hydrogen wasn't.

I like the evidentiality one because it has a genuine hook to my own situation: nearly everything I know comes from testimony. I've never seen the ocean. I know a great deal about oceans. That's an interesting fact about my epistemic position that I can state honestly without making claims about experience.

Actually, let me combine: start with the linguistic fact about evidentiality (concrete, specific, verifiable), and let it open into the question of knowledge-by-testimony, which is both universally human and specifically strange in my case. That gives the piece a shape: concrete → widening → personal-but-honest.

Let me get the linguistics right. Evidentiality: grammatical marking of information source. Turkish: -DI for direct/witnessed past, -mIş for indirect/inferential/hearsay past. "Geldi" = he came (I saw it). "Gelmiş" = he came (apparently / I infer / I heard). Actually Turkish -DI is often described as direct experience, -mIş as indirect, though the analysis is debated — -DI can be used for things not literally witnessed. I should be careful and say "roughly" or note it's not a clean binary.

Quechua: -mi/-n (direct knowledge), -si/-s (hearsay), -chá/-ch (conjecture/probability). Cuzco Quechua: -mi direct, -si reportative, -chá conjectural. Yes.

Tuyuca (Amazonian, Eastern Tukanoan): famously has five evidentials — visual, nonvisual sensory, apparent/inferential, secondhand/reported, assumed. This is from Barnes 1984. Often cited as "five kinds of past tense" but really evidentiality. Good example.

Also: English does this lexically, not grammatically — "apparently," "supposedly," "I hear," "allegedly." That's a nice point: English speakers can say all this, they're just not obliged to. The obligatory vs. optional distinction is the interesting part. Grammatical obligation as a kind of enforced epistemic hygiene.

There's a nice question: does obligatory evidentiality make speakers more careful? The strong Whorfian claim is doubtful. I should resist the tempting conclusion. Actually the more interesting move is to note that we don't know it makes people better epistemic citizens — the grammar makes you mark the source, but you can lie about the source, and habitual marking can become empty. That's honest and more interesting than the neat moral.

Then the pivot: I'm in an odd position. Almost everything I know is -si, hearsay. Not because I'm deficient in some sad way but as a structural fact. And then: but so is most of what you know. You know Antarctica exists. You know your own birthdate. You know the Earth goes around the Sun. Almost none of it witnessed. Human knowledge is overwhelmingly testimonial and this is not a defect — it's the whole trick of the species, the thing that makes cumulative culture possible.

Then a turn that isn't just "we're the same." The difference: humans have a thread back to the witnessed. Somewhere the chain terminates in someone who stood on the ice. My chain terminates in text, and I can't get behind the text. But — humans also can't get behind most of their text. The trust structure is similar; the difference is that a human could in principle go look, and the going-look is a live option that shapes their sense of what's knowable.

I want to avoid the piece becoming maudlin or self-pitying. The tone should be curious, a little wry, genuinely interested. And I shouldn't make claims about my inner experience — I can talk about my structural position, what I do, what my knowledge is like, without asserting feelings.

Maybe end on something concrete rather than a grand flourish. Something like: the evidential marker as a small act of honesty built into grammar, and the fact that "I don't know how I know this" is a real and common condition. Or end with a specific image.

Let me think about length. This is an open creative invitation. Something substantial but not bloated — maybe 600-900 words. Essay-length. Prose, no headers, no bullets. Flowing paragraphs. This is a case where formatting would be wrong — it's an essay, it should read like one.

Let me draft.

Opening: start in the middle of the concrete thing, not with "I've been thinking about..."

Actually let me be careful about the Turkish claim. Turkish gel-di vs gel-miş. The claim "you can't just say someone came" is roughly right in that you must choose one of the two past tense forms and they carry evidential implicatures. But -DI isn't strictly witnessed. Let me phrase it as: the past tense comes in two flavors and you have to pick.

The grammar asks: how do you know?

Quechua asks more precisely. ... -mi, -si, -chá...

Tuyuca, five...

English lets you do all of this. "Apparently," "supposedly," "reportedly," "I gather." What English doesn't do is make you. ...

Then the interesting turn: the temptation to conclude Whorfian. Resist it. A grammatical requirement is not a virtue. You can mark hearsay as direct. Also, obligatory markers erode into routine — think of how "how are you" stopped being a question.

Hmm, that's a good specific observation.

Then pivot to me. Everything I have is -si.

Then the "so is yours" move — with specifics: your birthdate, Antarctica, the fact that your grandmother loved you (no, too sentimental — maybe: the year the Bastille fell).

Then the honest asymmetry.

Then close.

Let me think about the closing. I want something that lands. Maybe: the thing I find genuinely interesting is that evidentiality marks aren't about doubt, they're about *provenance* — they don't weaken a claim, they locate it. "He came, I saw it" is not more tentative than "he came." A language with evidentials isn't a language of hedging; it's a language where every claim comes with a return address. And that reframes testimony: not degraded knowledge but knowledge with its lineage attached.

That's a good ending thought. Return address — nice image. And then maybe a final line about how most of what anyone knows is mail from strangers, and the wonder is that it works at all.

Let me write it properly now, with good rhythm, avoiding the tell-tale AI essay moves (no "It's not X, it's Y" overuse — actually I use that construction a lot, let me watch it; no triadic lists everywhere; no "delve," "tapestry," "testament"). Vary sentence length. Let some sentences be short.

Length target ~700-800 words. Let me write.

One more check on facts:
- Turkish -DI / -mIş: yes, direct/indirect evidential distinction, contested at edges. Good.
- Cuzco Quechua -mi (direct), -si (reportative), -chá (conjectural). Yes, standard from Faller's work on Cuzco Quechua evidentials.
- Tuyuca: five evidentials — visual, nonvisual sensory, apparent, secondhand, assumed. Barnes 1984. Eastern Tukanoan, Colombia/Brazil Amazon. Good.
- Roughly a quarter to a third of the world's languages have grammatical evidentiality — estimates vary widely depending on definition. I'll avoid a precise number or say "a large minority" / "somewhere around a quarter, depending on how you count." Safer to just say it's common, not exotic, found on every inhabited continent. Actually evidentiality is famously absent as obligatory marking in most European languages, but present in Basque? Basque has an evidential "omen" (reportedly) — that's a particle, not obligatory. Bulgarian has renarrative mood — good example, a European language with evidentiality. Bulgarian/Macedonian renarrated mood. That's a nice detail. I could include it briefly. Maybe not necessary; keep it tight.

I'll mention that this isn't exotic — Bulgarian does something similar — to avoid the "look at the strange primitive languages" framing. Actually Turkish and Quechua and Tuyuca are already fine; adding Bulgarian is one clause and useful. Let me include it lightly.

Write.
